hints: Notice $I_1$ is the total current through the cell and its internal resistance, while $I_2$ is only the current through the middle resistor in the upper parallel branch.
Closing the lower switch connects a second resistor in parallel with the middle resistor, so the combined external resistance $R$ decreases.
Link the larger $I_1$ to lost volts $I_1r$ inside the cell and to terminal p.d. $V = E - I_1r$ across the parallel resistors to decide what happens to $I_2 = V/R$.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit with the switch open: $I_1$ flows through the cell, internal resistance and the single middle resistor, so $I_1 = I_2$ initially.
Closing the switch adds the lower resistor in parallel with the middle resistor, so total external resistance $R$ decreases.
Use $I_1 = E/(R + r)$ where $E$ is e.m.f. and $r$ is internal resistance. Since $R$ decreases, the denominator decreases and $I_1$ increases.
The voltage across the parallel combination is the terminal p.d. $V = E - I_1r$. Because $I_1$ is larger, lost volts $I_1r$ is larger and $V$ is smaller.
For the fixed middle resistor of resistance $R_2$, $I_2 = V/R_2$. With smaller $V$ and unchanged $R_2$, $I_2$ decreases.
Therefore $I_1$ increases and $I_2$ decreases. This is option C.

options.A: Total external resistance falls when the second resistor is added in parallel, so total current $I_1$ increases, not decreases.
options.B: The parallel voltage is not fixed because increased $I_1$ increases lost volts in the internal resistance, so $I_2$ cannot stay the same.
options.C: Lower external resistance increases $I_1$, which increases lost volts $I_1r$ and lowers terminal p.d., so $I_2$ through the fixed middle resistor decreases.
options.D: $I_1$ does increase, but the terminal p.d. across the middle resistor falls, so $I_2$ decreases rather than staying the same.
